list.listitem: Screen for heart murmurs in childhood and as a part of the preparticipation examination for young athletes. C
Heart murmurs in childhood are common, and the great majority are benign. C
Most, but not all, congenital heart defects cause a heart murmur. C
No diagnostic testing is needed in a child with typical findings of an innocent murmur; echocardiography is not needed in most cases to differentiate an innocent from a pathologic murmur. C
Routine use of the chest x-ray is discouraged in the evaluation of a child with a heart murmur. C
ECG is highly specific but very insensitive; it is helpful when the murmur is abnormal, and unhelpful when the murmur is normal. B

Refer to a cardiologist any children who have a grade III or worse murmur; red flags such as exertional symptoms, cyanosis, clubbing, poor growth, poor feeding, or decreased femoral pulses; a harsh systolic murmur or a diastolic murmur; or an unusual sound such as a click, rub, gallop, or fixed split S2. C

background.definition: A cardiovascular murmur is more prolonged than a heart sound and is characterized according to timing in the cardiac cycle, intensity (loudness), frequency (pitch), configuration (shape), quality, duration, and direction of radiation.

list.listitem: Incidence of innocent murmurs, reportedly present in more than 50% of children between 2 and 7 years of age
Ventricular septal defect (VSD): 3 per 1000 live births
Atrial septal defect (ASD): 0.7 per 1000 live births
Aortic stenosis: 0.4 per 1000 live births
Pulmonic stenosis: 0.6 per 1000 live births
Coarctation of the aorta: 0.3 per 1000 live births
Patent ductus arteriosus: 0.5 per 1000 live births
Tetralogy of Fallot: 0.3 per 1000 live births
Innocent murmurs, not caused by any pathology

Other congenital heart defects
Innocent murmurs are caused by blood flow in a normal heart.
Flow across a stenotic semilunar valve (aortic or pulmonic) causes a systolic murmur, while flow across a stenotic atrioventricular valve (mitral or tricuspid) causes a diastolic murmur.

Regurgitation/insufficiency of a semilunar valve (aortic or pulmonic) causes a diastolic murmur, while regurgitation/insufficiency of an atrioventricular valve (mitral or tricuspid) causes a systolic murmur.
VSDs, and most other congenital heart defects, cause a systolic murmur.
Screening for heart murmurs in childhood is an essential component of the well-child physical exam. C

Preparticipation cardiovascular screening for student athletes prior to organized or competitive sports is recommended. Physical examination should include assessment for heart murmur, femoral pulses to exclude aortic coarctation, physical stigmata of Marfan syndrome, resting heart rate, and brachial artery blood pressure in the sitting position. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Vibratory quality of murmur, associated venous hum
Lower left sternal border, generally not radiating, harsh to blowing
Wide and fixed splitting of S2
Right upper sternal border radiating to carotids
Left upper sternal border radiating to back

list.listitem: Systolic murmurs are graded I to VI: I: faint; II: obvious; III: loud; IV: precordial thrill; V: heard with stethoscope on its side; and VI: heard with stethoscope not touching patient.
Diastolic murmurs are graded I to IV using the same definitions as above.

The history and physical of an expert examiner (pediatric cardiologist) is very accurate for distinguishing between innocent and pathologic murmurs in children. In one study of 161 children referred for asymptomatic heart murmur who had not yet been evaluated by a cardiologist, the cardiologist examination was 96% sensitive and 95% specific compared with echocardiography as the reference standard (LR+ 19.2, LR− 0.04). A second study confirmed these findings.

A murmur in an infant with feeding difficulty or poor weight gain, or in a child with chronic respiratory symptoms, is more concerning. The absence of these symptoms, however, does not offer significant reassurance that a murmur is innocent.
Children with a murmur and chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness, or syncope, particularly if exertional, should be referred to a pediatric cardiologist.

Defects that increase volume or pressure load to either LV or RV will increase precordial activity. The precordium is normally very quiet in young infants; an obvious precordial impulse is concerning for structural heart disease.
Grade I and II murmurs are likely to be innocent; most innocent murmurs are not loud, and most loud murmurs are not innocent.

Decreased femoral pulses are highly suggestive of coarctation of the aorta, and are an essential part of any well-child exam, and of the exam in a child with a murmur. Also a discrepancy between upper and lower extremity blood pressure suggests coarctation of the aorta. Lower extremity blood pressure is normally higher; obtaining accurate blood pressure in infants and young children can be difficult.

Wide and fixed splitting of S2 is pathognomonic for an ASD. This finding is typically subtle, and missed by inexperienced examiners. Diastolic murmurs are pathologic. Presence of either finding requires referral.

Physical examination alone is inadequate to detect mild cyanosis. Pulse oximetry is essential in the evaluation of a young infant with a murmur, and the child with abnormal pulse oximetry requires referral.

Chest radiography and electrocardiography are of limited value for distinguishing structural heart disease in children with a cardiac murmur. While an abnormal ECG is very specific, and indicates the likelihood of disease when abnormal, it has poor sensitivity. A normal ECG does not rule out structural heart disease.
Chest X-ray does not significantly alter the likelihood of disease when positive or negative; it is not recommended as a part of the routine assessment of the child with a heart murmur.
A cost-effectiveness analysis found that referral to a pediatric cardiologist is more cost effective than echocardiography ordered by the primary care physician.

On the other hand, a systematic review identified 12 studies with 1928 newborns with asymptomatic, non-syndromic cardiac murmur. All underwent echocardiogram, and 37% were diagnosed with congenital heart disease with ventricular septal defect being most common. Only 2.5% had severe congenital heart disease requiring immediate catheterization or surgery.
See for a suggested approach to the child with a heart murmur.
